title: When Prompts Override Vision: Instruction-Induced Hallucinations in LVLMs
claim: Models answer simple presence queries correctly but hallucinate plausible absent objects when instructions presuppose them; our fine-tuning fixes this.
layout: Image at left, three dashed Q&A boxes at right, color-coded answers
description: A wide figure. On the left is a street photo of a woman with an umbrella crossing a city street, with yellow taxis behind her. It has an orange dashed border and an image icon. On the right are three dashed rounded boxes with example Q&A for Qwen2-VL-7B. The green box at top left asks about a present car (answer Yes) and an absent pizza pan (answer No), with eye and magnifier icons. The yellow box at top right asks about an absent traffic light, and the model answers Yes or hedges with VCD. The blue box at the bottom asks a leading question about the color of the traffic light. The VCD model hallucinates 'yellow' in red text, while the HalluVL-DPO model correctly says there is no traffic light in green text. Object names are underlined, and red and green text mark wrong and right answers.
caption: Vision–language hallucination failure modes and mitigation. The model reliably recognizes present objects or the absence of random objects, but tends to hallucinate plausible yet absent (i.e., adversarial) objects, especially when the instruction presupposes their presence. Our HalluVL-DPO framework substantially mitigates this failure mode.
abstract: Despite impressive progress in capabilities of large vision-language models (LVLMs), these systems remain vulnerable to hallucinations, i.e., outputs that are not grounded in the visual input. Prior work has attributed hallucinations in LVLMs to factors such as limitations of the vision backbone or the dominance of the language component, yet the relative importance of these factors remains unclear. To resolve this ambiguity, We propose HalluScope, a benchmark to better understand the extent to which different factors induce hallucinations. Our analysis indicates that hallucinations largely stem from excessive reliance on textual priors and background knowledge, especially information introduced through textual instructions. To mitigate hallucinations induced by textual instruction priors, we propose HalluVL-DPO, a framework for fine-tuning off-the-shelf LVLMs towards more visually grounded responses. HalluVL-DPO leverages preference optimization using a curated training dataset that we construct, guiding the model to prefer grounded responses over hallucinated ones. We demonstrate that our optimized model effectively mitigates the targeted hallucination failure mode, while preserving or improving performance on other hallucination benchmarks and visual capability evaluations. To support reproducibility and further research, we will publicly release our evaluation benchmark, preference training dataset, and code.
